nameStory: The Thick-spined Jumping Spider gets its name from the robust, thick spines that project from its legs, which are noticeably stouter than those of its close relatives. These spines help distinguish it from the Thin-spined Jumping Spider, which has more delicate, slender leg spines. The name is straightforward and practical - exactly what early spider researchers needed to tell similar species apart!
description: The Thick-spined Jumping Spider is a small but active hunter that stalks its prey rather than building webs to catch food. Like all jumping spiders, it has excellent vision thanks to its large, forward-facing eyes and can leap several times its body length to catch insects or escape danger. This species is relatively small, typically measuring less than half an inch in body length. Its compact, robust build and distinctive leg spines make it recognizable among the jumping spider family.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Compact and sturdy with a relatively thick abdomen and robust legs that feel substantial when gently examined

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Four large eyes across the front of the face like tiny black jewels, with the middle pair being especially prominent and giving an alert, intelligent expression

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Moves in quick, jerky motions and will often turn to face you directly when approached, appearing curious rather than fleeing immediately

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Body length typically under 0.5 inches, small enough to sit comfortably on a dime with legs slightly extended

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Variable coloration but often with subtle patterns on the abdomen and a somewhat iridescent quality to the body that shifts in different lighting

habitat: Found in various habitats throughout New England, from woodland edges to gardens and meadows. They prefer areas with plenty of surfaces to hunt on, such as tree bark, fallen logs, rock walls, and even the sides of buildings. Look for them in sunny spots where flying insects are active, as they need good hunting grounds.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, emerging to hunt small insects awakening from winter dormancy. Males may begin courtship displays with their characteristic leg-waving dances.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most commonly seen hunting during warm, sunny days. Mating occurs and females may be found guarding small silk egg sacs under bark or stones.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall, with spiderlings dispersing from egg sacs. Adults prepare for winter by seeking sheltered locations under bark or leaf litter.
seasonality.winter: Overwinter as juveniles or adults in protected spots like loose bark, rock crevices, or leaf litter, becoming dormant until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Jumping spiders have better color vision than most mammals and can see into the ultraviolet spectrum, meaning they see a completely different world of colors and patterns on flowers and other spiders that are invisible to human eyes!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small jumping spiders, but the thick leg spines are diagnostic if you can get a close look. Remember: thick spines = Thick-spined Jumping Spider. Other jumping spiders in the area will have more delicate, hair-like leg projections.
compareHints: The Thick-spined Jumping Spider differs from Hart's Jumping Spider and the Thin-spined Jumping Spider primarily in the robustness of its leg spines - they're noticeably thicker and more substantial. While all three species share the typical jumping spider body plan and behavior, the spine thickness is the most reliable way to distinguish between them. The Thin-spined species has delicate, almost hair-like spines, while Hart's Jumping Spider has intermediate spine thickness.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Hart's Jumping Spider differs from its close relatives like the Thin-spined Jumping Spider by having a more robust, stocky build rather than an elongated appearance.
Among its Tutelina relatives in New England, the Thin-spined Jumping Spider is distinguished by its delicate leg spines compared to the robust spines of the Thick-spined Jumping Spider.
Distinguishing between Tutelina species requires very close examination and is challenging even for experts.
